full_text:
Continuous high-resolution monitoring of subtropical xerophytic forests in central Argentina demonstrates that soil water availability serves as the primary environmental filter governing whether extreme heat waves translate into acute stem dehydration and radial growth cessation in Neltuma affinis. Field observations conducted over a complete annual cycle revealed that thermal extremes do not act in isolation upon tree hydraulic function; rather, their physiological impact depends directly on antecedent soil moisture conditions. During summer monitoring, severe thermal anomalies operating concurrently with depleted soil moisture reserves produced pronounced stem shrinkage, collapsed the diurnal hydration-dehydration cycle, and elevated tree water deficit to seasonal maximums. Conversely, when identical or comparable heat wave thresholds occurred under conditions of abundant soil water, elevated moisture buffered near-surface soil heating, supported nocturnal stem rehydration, and prevented measurable reductions in stem diameter. These empirical findings demonstrate that heat wave vulnerability in this dominant woody taxon is mediated by compound hydrothermal stress rather than by elevated ambient temperature alone.
The study was situated within an observational context of documented long-term regional warming based on continuous meteorological records compiled between 1935 and 2025 at the INTA EEA Paraná observatory. Over this ninety-year instrumental record, regional mean annual air temperature exhibited a statistically significant warming rate of 0.14 degrees Celsius per decade. Meteorological screening identified a total of 101 heat wave events, 76 percent of which occurred after 1985, reflecting an intensifying frequency that increased by 14 percent per decade under a Poisson model. Comparative assessment of thirty-year climatological blocks revealed that heat wave frequency rose from 0.37 events per year between 1935 and 1965 to 0.79 events per year between 1995 and 2025. Beyond occurrence rates, the structural severity of these thermal spells, evaluated through heat wave magnitude indices calculated from daily maximum and minimum air temperatures, reached historical peaks during the 2015 to 2025 interval, driven primarily by prolonged event durations and heightened persistence of elevated nighttime minimum temperatures.
Field investigations focused on Neltuma affinis, formerly classified as Prosopis affinis and commonly known as ñandubay, a heliophilous tree within the Fabaceae family that forms dominant canopy components across the xerophytic woodlands of the Espinal phytogeographic province. The experimental site was established within the El Guayabo protected natural area in Villaguay, located within Entre Ríos Province, Argentina. The local soil profile is classified as fine, smectitic, thermic Typic Hapluderts, presenting a silty clay loam A1 horizon extending approximately 12 centimeters deep over a dense, low-permeability B2 horizon containing 50 to 55 percent smectitic clay. These Vertisols exhibit pronounced shrink-swell dynamics characterized by slickensides and wide desiccation cracks reaching up to two centimeters across dry periods. While providing high potential water storage, the strong matric forces exerted by smectitic clays severely restrict root moisture extraction under drying conditions, amplifying environmental water stress during periods of high evaporative demand.
To capture fine-scale physiological and environmental dynamics, automated point dendrometers were installed at breast height on six healthy, socially dominant Neltuma affinis trees exhibiting trunk diameters between 12.6 and 26.4 centimeters. Stem radius variations were recorded at fifteen-minute intervals from 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025, operating alongside automated Campbell CS650 sensors monitoring soil temperature and volumetric water content at a depth of 30 centimeters. Analysis of expressed population signal approaching the 0.85 benchmark and mean inter-series correlation exceeding 0.46 confirmed a coherent stand-level environmental signal among monitored stems. Soil volumetric water content was calibrated against laboratory pressure-plate determinations of permanent wilting point at minus 1500 kilopascals, establishing an absolute lower reference threshold of 0.28 cubic meters per cubic meter. These measurements were converted into relative extractable water indices to quantify biologically available soil moisture reserves accessible for tree uptake.
Seasonal stem trajectories demonstrated a pronounced bimodal expansion pattern closely coupled to fluctuating soil water availability. Radial expansion commenced in early October and peaked in late November under favorable moisture conditions, but abruptly transitioned into sustained stem contraction that lasted over two months from mid-December through mid-February. This contraction coincided with a severe summer drought that drove soil volumetric water content down to 0.296 cubic meters per cubic meter, closely approaching the permanent wilting point. Low soil moisture content enhanced daily soil thermal amplitude, allowing maximum soil temperatures at 30 centimeters depth to exceed 42 degrees Celsius across five distinct days. Stem diameters remained severely compressed throughout January and early February until substantial precipitation in mid-February restored soil moisture, precipitating rapid stem rehydration and renewed radial expansion that re-established stem baselines attained before drought onset.
Within the monitored growing cycle, three discrete heat wave events were recorded, each displaying contrasting atmospheric demand and antecedent edaphic conditions. The first event, occurring between 105 and 109 days after growth onset, lasted five days with a mean vapor pressure deficit of 4.2 kilopascals and generated cumulative heat wave magnitude index values reflecting prolonged thermal persistence. The second event, occurring between 131 and 134 days after growth onset, proved exceptionally intense, recording mean maximum air temperatures of 38 degrees Celsius and atmospheric vapor pressure deficits reaching 5.0 kilopascals. Both episodes developed on dry soils where relative extractable water had dropped below 10 percent and 30 percent one week prior, subsequently falling to 1 percent and 5 percent during the events. These compound hot-dry conditions exposed trees to simultaneous hydraulic strain from desiccated soil reserves and intense atmospheric drying power.
To resolve the distinct contributions of soil drying and elevated temperature, daily normalized stem radius variations from December through March were analyzed using regularized dynamic linear regression models incorporating autoregressive terms and lagged hydroclimatic variables across a one-week memory window. The ridge regression model achieved strong predictive fit, yielding an R-squared of 0.966 and a root mean square error of 0.170 standard deviations. Counterfactual event simulations, which held soil temperatures at normalized zero while maintaining observed soil moisture, revealed that for the first heat wave, maximum soil temperature produced an estimated cumulative contraction of minus 0.831 standard deviations, whereas volumetric water content contributed minus 1.097 standard deviations. During the second event, maximum soil temperature induced a cumulative effect of minus 0.960 standard deviations compared to minus 0.997 standard deviations from volumetric water content, verifying that soil water depletion exerted equal or greater control over stem shrinkage than thermal anomalies.
Analysis of high-resolution hydraulic indicators derived from normalized maximum daily stem shrinkage and normalized tree water deficit revealed profound disruption of internal stem water reserves during the two compound heat wave events. Normalizing both parameters by the 99th percentile of maximum shrinkage standardized individual response differences, allowing precise identification of periods when predawn water deficit exceeded daily shrinkage capacity. Under compound heat wave conditions, predawn normalized tree water deficit values surged, reaching overall mean maximum levels of 1.178 plus or minus 0.246 and averaging 0.88 plus or minus 0.15 during the February event. Concurrently, diurnal stem shrinkage amplitudes collapsed toward minimal values because depleted soil water supplies prevented nighttime stem rehydration. This lack of nocturnal recovery prevented elastic tissues from replenishing water lost to residual transpiration, depressing cambial turgor below levels required for active wood cell division and expansion.
A critical internal control was provided by the third documented heat wave occurring between 144 and 147 days after growth onset. While satisfying standard meteorological criteria for a heat wave, this late February episode was preceded by heavy rainfall events totaling 131 millimeters over four days that restored relative extractable water to 0.801, representing over 80 percent of extractable capacity. With soil volumetric water content sustained above 0.543 cubic meters per cubic meter, maximum soil temperatures during the event reached only 33.4 degrees Celsius. Consequently, the third heat wave failed to produce marked stem contraction, elevated tree water deficit, or detectable growth reductions in the monitored cohort. This marked contrast provides direct field validation that high air temperatures cannot trigger severe stem dehydration when adequate soil water reserves buffer near-surface root temperatures and sustain evaporative cooling and overnight stem recharge.
Despite strong stand-level synchrony, monitored trees displayed notable intraspecific variation in response magnitude. Tree NEAF02 experienced the most extreme water deficits across both summer heat waves and exhibited substantially depressed leaf flush during the subsequent 2025 to 2026 season, indicating persistent physiological strain. In contrast, the smallest individual, NEAF04, maintained radial expansion rates nearly twice the stand average, suggesting that ontogenetic stage, rooting depth, or microhabitat variations modulate vulnerability. The authors emphasize that while all monitored trees survived through prompt post-drought rehydration, increasing regional heat wave recurrence and longer event durations could outpace nocturnal recovery margins. By establishing that soil water availability governs whether heat extremes cause physiological cessation, continuous dendrometer monitoring offers a sensitive operational framework for tracking early warning signals of forest decline across vulnerable Espinal ecosystems facing projected climate warming.

full_text:
By Damilola Aina
The United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has warned that the world is running out of time to contain the climate crisis.
Guterres called for an accelerated transition from fossil fuels, increased climate financing and urgent action to protect vulnerable countries from worsening global warming.
The Secretary-General on Wednesday said global emissions needed to decline by approximately six per cent annually, warning that existing national climate commitments were insufficient to prevent dangerous temperature increases, despite growing investments in renewable energy.
He urged developed countries to deliver at least $300bn annually in climate finance by 2035, ensuring that the wider $1.3tn financing ambition translated into actual funding for developing countries that are still working to improve their industrial capacity, infrastructure, income levels, healthcare, education and living standards.
He stated, “Developed countries must lead in delivering at least $300 billion a year by 2035, and set out concrete plans with clear milestones to at least triple adaptation finance by then.
“The $1.3tn goal must become real finance flowing to developing countries and this demands that every source of finance pull its weight.”
Guterres spoke at the World Leaders Summit of the ongoing 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye, where Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed also called for stronger international cooperation, climate financing and practical interventions to address the crisis.
The World Leaders Summit at COP31 brings together heads of state and government, alongside senior international officials, to discuss urgent climate challenges, strengthen global cooperation and translate climate commitments into concrete action.
The summit, attended by our correspondent, opened with a 30-minute cultural performance celebrating Türkiye’s heritage, featuring the renowned Fire of Anatolia dance ensemble.
The performance brought together traditional folk dances, music, colourful costumes and contemporary choreography to portray the historical meeting of civilisations in Anatolia.
The presentation reflected the region’s position as a historical crossroads between Europe and Asia, where different cultures, trade routes and civilisations have interacted over centuries.
The Fire of Anatolia, established in 1999, is known for combining traditional Anatolian folk dances with ballet and modern dance to promote cultural unity and peace.
The cultural display provided an opening message of coexistence and cooperation ahead of the leaders’ discussions on a climate crisis that increasingly requires countries to work across political and economic differences.
Addressing the summit, Guterres said the world must confront the reality that climate change was advancing faster than governments’ responses.
“Our first climate duty is to tell the truth. The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. Emissions in 2025 reached all-time highs. Heat records keep shattering. The last four years were the hottest ever,” he said.
He criticised fossil fuel interests for continuing to profit from activities contributing to global warming, warning that climate disasters were increasingly destroying lives, livelihoods and economies.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby, but fossil fuels do,” Guterres said in Turkey at his final UN climate summit as secretary-general.
He recalled that countries had pledged under the 2015 Paris Agreement to limit global temperature increases to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, but said scientific evidence suggested that a temporary overshoot was now inevitable.
However, he argued that the prospect of exceeding the target should not become an excuse for inaction.
“Science tells us an overshoot above that level is now inevitable. But science is not telling us to surrender. It’s telling us to fight harder.
“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be. We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence,” he said.
The UN chief identified three major lessons from the past decade, including the rapid growth of renewable energy, the declining economic case for fossil fuels and the slow pace of global climate action.
He noted that solar energy, which accounted for only one per cent of global electricity generation a decade ago, had become a major contributor to meeting rising electricity demand, while electric vehicles were also gaining market share.
He said three-quarters of humanity lived in countries importing fossil fuels, leaving them exposed to international price shocks and energy insecurity.
“The case for fossil fuels is collapsing. Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels. Hostage to price shocks they did not create and they cannot control,” he said.
Guterres called for a just and orderly transition to renewable energy, including ending new coal development, reducing methane emissions and expanding electricity grids, energy storage and clean electrification.
He also demanded a new climate justice compact, arguing that developing countries were being denied the financial resources needed to implement climate commitments.
He said emerging and developing economies outside China accounted for nearly two-thirds of the world’s population but received less than one-fifth of global clean energy investments, while borrowing costs in many of those countries were two to three times higher.
He also criticised the imbalance between profits made by oil companies and resources available to countries suffering climate-related losses.
“In the last quarter alone, the nine largest oil companies pocketed $95bn in profits. Meanwhile, the Loss and Damage Fund has received around $600m. That is what these companies made in about 14 hours,” he said, calling for taxes on windfall profits from fossil fuel companies to support vulnerable countries.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who is leading the COP31 negotiations alongside Türkiye’s hosting arrangement, said the conference must translate climate commitments into practical results, particularly for Pacific island countries threatened by rising sea levels.
He recalled meeting a 13-year-old student, Melalusi Soketia, in Tuvalu, who feared for the future of her home despite dreaming of becoming a doctor.
Reading her message to world leaders, Albanese said, “We all have one simple dream, to grow up safely here in Tuvalu, the place we call home. We are not asking for pity, we are asking for help and partnership. Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”
He said the average elevation of Tuvalu’s islands was just 1.83 metres above sea level, making coastal communities particularly vulnerable to storm surges and rising oceans.
Albanese said Australia had doubled renewable electricity generation in six years, with renewables now accounting for half of its electricity mix.
He also disclosed that more than 600,000 home batteries had been installed in the country in the past year.
He called for increased investment in clean energy, electrification, ocean protection and climate adaptation, particularly for vulnerable countries.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, whose country is expected to host COP32 in 2027, said climate action must be treated as an economic development priority rather than an environmental commitment alone.
He explained that droughts and floods associated with changing weather patterns were affecting agricultural production, displacing families and threatening livelihoods in Ethiopia.
He said, “In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy.”
Abiy disclosed that more than 90 per cent of Ethiopia’s electricity came from hydropower, making climate resilience and diversification of energy sources critical to its economic stability.
He said the country was expanding wind, solar and geothermal power while using satellite technology and artificial intelligence to improve weather forecasting and provide farmers with early warnings.
The Ethiopian leader also highlighted the country’s Green Legacy Initiative, through which more than 56 billion seedlings had been planted to restore degraded land, expand forests and create employment.
He said Ethiopia had banned imports of petrol- and diesel-powered cars as part of its transition to electric mobility, adding that climate financing must be released early enough to help vulnerable communities prepare for extreme weather.
On Ethiopia’s preparations to host COP32, he challenged international financiers to make their commitments measurable.
“That work should begin here, with every Pledge of Finance answering three questions. How much? By when? On what terms? The answers must be clear enough for a government to budget, an investor to commit, and a community to prepare,” he said.

Following a record 21-day heatwave across sub-Arctic Fennoscandia in July 2025, researchers at Umeå University are preparing to recreate indoor summer heat to investigate how older adults respond physically and psychologically inside homes designed for cold winters. The 2026–2030 project will combine controlled heat exposure, physiological measurements and brain-activity monitoring to evaluate adaptations such as shading and ventilation, with the aim of identifying measures that protect well-being without assuming that the same solutions work for every household.
For decades, homes in northern Sweden have been built primarily to withstand long, cold winters. Insulation, energy-efficient windows and building envelopes that limit heat loss help maintain warmth when outdoor temperatures are low. During a summer heatwave, however, the same homes can be difficult to keep cool. The research question now being pursued at Umeå University is how that indoor environment affects older residents and whether relatively accessible building adaptations can reduce heat-related discomfort and psychological strain.
The challenge is not simply to establish that extreme heat can affect health. Researchers already have evidence linking temperature exposure with physical and mental-health outcomes, but less is known about how older people respond to specific indoor conditions and which interventions produce measurable improvements. Umeå University’s new project will examine the interaction between the building, the occupant and the measures available to reduce heat exposure, rather than treating outdoor weather conditions as a complete measure of the environment people experience at home.
The 2025 heatwave provides a recent example of the conditions motivating the research. According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the World Meteorological Organization, sub-Arctic Fennoscandia experienced its most severe heatwave on record in July 2025. The event lasted 21 days, from July 12 to August 1, with temperatures reaching or exceeding 30°C (86°F) in parts of the region close to and within the Arctic Circle. The highest reported temperature was 34.9°C (94.8°F) at Frosta in Norway. The regional severity ranking combines temperature anomaly, duration and the area affected, rather than relying on the highest temperature alone.
Copernicus attributes the prolonged heat to a persistent atmospheric blocking pattern over northern Europe. In this configuration, a high-pressure system remained between areas of lower pressure, allowing unusually warm and sunny conditions to persist. At high northern latitudes, where summer daylight lasts for much of the day, the resulting weather pattern sustained high temperatures over an extended period. The regional heatwave was accompanied by dry conditions, elevated fire danger and unusually warm seawater in parts of the surrounding seas.
A separate study by Feng et al. (2026), involving researchers from Umeå University, examined how residents responded to that 2025 Nordic heatwave. The investigation collected survey data from 201 households representing 450 residents in Umeå, Skellefteå and Luleå. It assessed reported thermal discomfort, perceived risk, psychological effects, household care responsibilities and the adaptations residents used during the event. Unlike the newly announced laboratory project, this was a completed survey-based investigation of an actual heatwave.
The survey found that behavioural changes were considerably more common than purchasing cooling equipment. Among the surveyed households, 94.0% reported adopting daily behavioural measures, while 22.4% reported purchasing new cooling devices. The distinction matters because changing routines and making purchases involve different costs and resources. The study also found that respondents with age-, health-, socioeconomic- or housing-related vulnerabilities continued to report greater heat-related impacts despite more active behavioural adaptation.
Those findings provide relevant background, but they cannot establish that a particular household intervention reduced physiological or psychological harm. The survey relied on reported experiences and behaviours, and its results describe associations among household characteristics, responses and perceived impacts. Its 450 residents were not exclusively older adults. The new Umeå project will address a narrower question by comparing controlled indoor heat conditions and potential adaptations while recording direct physiological measurements and participants’ assessments.
There is also a wider scientific reason to investigate mental well-being alongside physical responses. Ugwu et al. (2026) reviewed 28 quantitative studies of climate exposures and mental or cognitive health among adults older than 60. Their analysis found associations between thermal stress, including heat and cold exposure, and increased depressive symptoms. The authors also identified emerging evidence connecting heat exposure with cognitive impairment, although the underlying studies differed considerably in their methods and outcome measurements.
The review identified a pronounced geographic imbalance in the research literature. Of the 28 included studies, 12 were conducted in East Asia, including 11 in China, while only one eligible study came from Europe. The authors did not conduct a single pooled statistical estimate for all outcomes because of differences among the included studies. Their conclusions support further investigation of thermal exposure and mental health, but they do not establish that every older person responds in the same way or that all exposure conditions have equivalent effects.
The newly announced Umeå investigation is titled Ageing at Home During Heatwaves in Northern Sweden: Protecting Mental Well-being through Evidence-Based Indoor Climate Adaptation. It is led by Weizhuo Lu, professor at the Department of Applied Physics and Electronics and director of the Intelligent Human-Buildings Interaction Lab (IHBI). The programme runs from 2026 to 2030 and brings together building research, psychology and neuroscience to examine how older residents experience heat inside homes.
Umeå University announced the project on November 5, 2026, reporting nearly SEK 9 million in support from Formas, the Swedish research council for sustainable development. Formas lists the project under reference 2026-01293 with an amount of SEK 8 978 276 in its preliminary decision table. The funding authority specifies that only decisions published through its Prisma system guarantee granted funding, a qualification that applies to the amount shown in the publicly available table.
The IHBI laboratory combines a physical climate chamber with immersive virtual environments. The chamber provides a setting in which indoor temperature, humidity and airflow can be controlled, while the virtual system can make the surroundings appear to resemble an ordinary home. This arrangement allows participants to experience physical indoor conditions while interacting with a simulated living environment. The research team can then compare responses across different settings without depending entirely on the timing of naturally occurring heatwaves.
The laboratory is equipped with physiological sensors and technology for recording brain activity through electroencephalography (EEG). EEG measures electrical activity using electrodes placed on the scalp. The researchers plan to combine these records with wearable physiological measurements, behavioural observations and participants’ own reports of comfort, stress, fatigue and mental well-being. These different measurements are complementary: changes in recorded brain activity or physiological signals alone do not establish a person’s psychological state or demonstrate that an adaptation has improved mental health.
Lu’s research description outlines a repeated-measures experimental approach in which participants are compared under thermally neutral conditions, during heat exposure and under adaptation conditions. Studying the same people across different environments can help distinguish responses to changing indoor conditions from differences between individuals. The strength of the resulting conclusions will nevertheless depend on the experimental protocol, participant characteristics, exposure conditions and the consistency of the measurements obtained.
The physical characteristics of northern Swedish housing are central to the project. Buildings designed to retain heat often have insulated walls, efficient windows and ventilation arrangements developed primarily for cold-weather energy performance. Those features do not, by themselves, determine how hot an individual room will become. Solar exposure, shading, ventilation practices and the building’s ability to release accumulated heat can also affect indoor conditions. The researchers intend to examine how variations in housing and occupant circumstances influence responses to summer heat.
Solar shading and ventilation are among the adaptations Umeå University identifies for evaluation. Shading can reduce the amount of solar energy entering a room through windows, while ventilation can exchange indoor and outdoor air when conditions permit. The effectiveness of either measure depends on the circumstances in which it is used. The new project has not yet established which combination provides the greatest benefit to older adults or whether an improvement in thermal comfort produces a corresponding change in measured stress or mental well-being.
The research also considers differences in the resources available to older residents. Mobility limitations, household finances, housing characteristics and social support can influence whether a person can alter their indoor environment or obtain assistance during prolonged heat. A measure that can be installed or operated easily in one home may be difficult to use in another. Umeå University said the resulting guidance will be developed in dialogue with older residents, relatives, senior citizens’ organisations and Umeå Municipality, with the aim of making recommendations accessible to households with differing needs.
The research team includes Weizhuo Lu and Kailun Feng from Umeå University’s Department of Applied Physics and Electronics, alongside Linus Andersson, Johan Eriksson and Gustaf Wadenholt from the Department of Psychology. The university’s November 5 press-release distribution indicated that small-scale internal pilot tests were expected to begin in early December 2026 or January 2027. Those dates describe anticipated research activities, not completed experimental findings.
The principal scientific question remains how reliably responses observed in a controlled laboratory can inform decisions inside real homes. The 2025 heatwave survey documented how residents reported coping with prolonged heat, while the broader systematic review identified mental and cognitive health associations across different climate exposures. The Umeå experiments are intended to test the next part of that problem: whether measurable changes in indoor conditions can reduce heat-related strain among older adults, which measures perform best, and how those effects vary between people and housing circumstances. The project has not yet reported results resolving those questions.

Open Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, La Gomera and El Hierro The orange-level warnings have expired, and the severe weather situation is therefore changing.
On Wednesday, the orange alert will remain in force only for La Palma. The AEMET has issued a warning for the whole island from 10.00 am until midnight, forecasting heavy rain of up to 30 millimetres in an hour, with the meteorological office putting the probability at between 40 and 70 per cent.
According to the authorities, the heavy rain is mainly affecting the areas of Breña Baja, Breña Alta and Santa Cruz de La Palma. In addition, there are two yellow rain warnings forecasting up to 60 millimetres of rain in twelve hours: the first applies to the west of the island and has been in force since 7 am, the second to the mountainous region and the east from 6 pm. Both remain in force until midnight.
Since last night, the situation on La Palma has changed several times. In the early hours of the morning, AEMET raised the wind warning for La Palma to red, whilst an orange warning was already in place due to heavy rain. The yellow rain warnings for the other islands remain in place until Thursday.
A yellow rain warning is in force on Tenerife until Thursday morning
On Tenerife, the wind had been at orange alert since Tuesday evening, before the island later became the first to drop back to yellow. The whole island is now on yellow alert due to rain, from 10.00 on Wednesday until 7.59 on Thursday. The AEMET is forecasting up to 15 millimetres in an hour; the probability is the same as on La Palma. According to the weather service, showers in the north of the island are particularly likely to be accompanied by thunderstorms.
The yellow warning is in force from 10.00 on Wednesday until 11.59 on Thursday, including on Gran Canaria, Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, with rainfall of up to 15 millimetres per hour. Thunderstorms are not ruled out by the AEMET, particularly on the easternmost islands. El Hierro and La Gomera will see the situation ease sooner, despite the same amount of rainfall; there, the yellow warning ends on Thursday at 4.59 am.
Rain and thunderstorms can cause large volumes of water to be released in the higher elevations of La Palma and Gran Canaria, which then flow down through the barrancos to the coast. You should therefore exercise particular caution in the ravines and their immediate surroundings.
